title: [Master Express Lesson 1] Get on board! Learn the first lesson of rendering well, the CLO Master Express is departing~
description:
Xiao C wishes everyone a happy Dragon Boat Festival holiday! This time, the replay is released early~
Master Express — The live replay of the rendering interface features introduction is here! Hurry up and practice to keep up with the expert's pace!
transcript:
Welcome to today’s live broadcast.  
Welcome to today’s live broadcast.  
Welcome to today’s live broadcast.  

Today’s live broadcast topic is rendering, so we will give a detailed introduction to rendering-related functions.  
Now, let’s begin today’s live broadcast.  

Sorry, I forgot to introduce myself. I am the host today, I’m Yingyin. Welcome everyone to support and watch my live broadcast.  

Now, let’s take a look at rendering. It is located in the main menu. By clicking on “Render,” you can find some rendering-related operations.  

Since we updated the 3D window’s rendering engine in version 5.2,  
we can see the rendering engine in the 3D window.  
In the 3D window’s context menu, the first icon shows a high-quality rendered 3D window.  
Clicking it will enable this function.  

After enabling it, you can see the high-quality rendered 3D effect.  
Let’s compare it after turning it off.  

This is the ordinary 3D window, this is the high-quality rendered window,  
and this is the final rendered image. We can compare them through this image.  

The first is a snapshot from the ordinary 3D window.  
The middle one is a snapshot with high-quality rendered 3D enabled.  
Finally, this is the ultimate rendered image. You can choose according to your needs.  

Next, we can record a rotating video from the main menu under “File.”  
We can enable the high-quality rendering function,  
so that the recorded rotating video will have a better rendering effect.  

Here, you can adjust the direction of the video  
and its duration, then click “Record.”  

Now, the 3D window starts recording the rotating video.  
The duration means how long it takes for one full rotation.  

The longer the duration, the slower the rotation speed will be.  
This way, our rotation video recording is complete.  

We can click “Play” to preview the video.  
Once confirmed, click “Save” to save the rotation video.  

Now, name the file.  
This is an AVI format video.  
The video is now being saved.  

Let’s check the effect of the high-quality rendered rotation video.  
Thanks to the optimization of the 3D window rendering engine, we can quickly record a rotation video with a good effect.  
The speed is very fast.  

Next, let’s close this.  

Now, let’s focus on introducing the rendering window.  
Open the rendering window to take a look.  

At the top of the rendering window, there is a row of rendering toolbars.  
Let’s first click the first icon on the first row, which is the synchronous rendering function.  
It can refresh the rendering.  

This is the preview of the rendering window.  
Synchronous rendering lets you see the rendering effect in real time.  
You can view the rendered effect live in the preview window.  

The second icon is final rendering.  
After adjusting all parameters, clicking this starts the final render.  
So don’t forget this step.  

Currently, it is grayed out and cannot be clicked,  
because synchronous rendering is enabled.  
We must first click “Stop Rendering”  
before we can perform the final rendering.  

Now, after clicking “Stop Rendering,” the final render icon becomes selectable.  
Clicking it will start the final rendering process.  

So, don’t forget this step when doing rendering.  

Now, the image has been rendered.  
Open the folder to see the rendered image.  
This is the final rendering effect.  

What else is the final rendering for?  
If we have clicked “Stop Rendering,” what is its use?  
Sometimes, after clicking the final render icon,  
you may find that the clothing needs some adjustment,  
such as changing color or modifying details.  

We can stop the rendering to make modifications promptly.  
After clicking final render, a progress bar appears at the top right showing rendering progress.  
If you need to stop, just click “Stop.”  

This is the stop rendering function.  

The fourth icon is to copy the current image.  
We can copy the image in the preview window.  

Let’s do synchronous rendering first.  
Now, click “Copy Current Image” to copy it out.  

If you are working on a spreadsheet, such as Excel,  
you can paste the copied image into the spreadsheet for other uses.  
You can adjust the image size and save it into the spreadsheet.  

This is the “Copy Current Image” function.  

Next, the fifth icon is to save the current image.  
Earlier, we only copied it out.  
This saves the image from the preview window directly.  

You don’t need to wait for the final rendering effect.  
If you just want the preview image, you can save it directly.  

Name the file now.  
Now you can see the saved image from the preview window.  
This is not the final rendering image.  
So its clarity and quality are not as high as the final render.  
Please note this point.  

Next, the sixth icon opens the saved folder.  
This lets us quickly locate the saved files.  

Here is the path of the saved folder we mentioned earlier.  

The seventh icon is image/video properties.  
There are many parameters here for adjustment.  

First, you can open or save an image/video property file.  
Click “Open” to load previously adjusted parameters for use.  

Next, you can choose whether to render an image or an animation.  

Here, I will choose “Image” first, meaning rendering a single image.  
“Current view” means the current state of the 3D window.  
“Cosmo view” is a user-defined view.  

Choose user-defined view.  
After opening, a dialog appears with the user’s views in the 3D window.  
Here, you can set the desired view according to preference.  

You can open a previously saved user view file or save the current view file.  

On the right, there is a camera for the current view.  
Click the camera to record the current view.  

Next, I rotate to the side view.  
Click the camera again to record the side view.  
Click the camera again to record the back view.  

Finally, if you want to add detail, zoom in the 3D window and click the camera again.  

In this way, I have saved four user-defined views.  
After saving, the system will follow these views to render multiple images at once.  

You can render all views with your chosen style.  
If you have one, you can load it here.  

You can choose the image size here.  
I use 1920x1080, which matches my display.  

Next is the direction: vertical or horizontal.  
Let’s refresh by synchronizing first.  
You’ll see the frame outside the image.  

Switch to horizontal and observe the effect.  
This can be chosen according to your style.  
Pay attention to the image border.  

Next is width, ratio, and pixels.  
No need to adjust if not necessary.  

You can choose the background color, including transparency.  
I had transparency enabled but will now turn it off.  

Now the rendered image has a background.  
A new feature allows you to use textures as backgrounds.  
Click the square to show the background.  

The system has many background textures, about 14.  
Choose one randomly.  
Click to switch back to the front view I recorded.  
The preview now shows the background texture.  

You can choose the file name and username.  
The file name is based on the project file name.  
The path is the folder mentioned earlier.  
You can also find the saved path here.  

You can choose the image format as needed: PNG or JPG.  
There is also an HTML file that can be used in web browsers.  
You can embed this file in your website.  

Now I click it.  

After setting all parameters, go back.  
Click to stop rendering.  
This is how to perform final rendering.  

After clicking final rendering, the system renders images from four defined angles at once.  

Now, we have four views.  
Here you can see the rendering progress bar and the rendering time.  

Look at the final rendering results.  
Check the back and special views by clicking next.  

This is the HTML file and the resource folder where images are saved.  

Next, let’s talk about rotating images.  
You can choose the number of images, with many options available.  
You can also set a custom number, for example, 12 images for a full 360° rotation.  

Choose the rotation direction: clockwise or counterclockwise.  
Save the video.  

If you want to rotate the video, select this option.  
This produces not only 12 rotation images but also a video.  

You can adjust the total recording time, i.e., how long it takes to complete one rotation.  
Next is the duration of each single image.  

I’ll stop here for now.  

Next is the image size, which I covered earlier.  
The following parameters are the same.  

Next, animation rendering.  
You can render animation here, provided you have completed it in animation mode.  

Choose the rendering area: full or play area.  
Remember to select “Save Video” to get a complete video.  

Frames per second is usually set to 30.  
Choose the direction according to your style.  
I’ll change it to horizontal.  

Synchronize rendering and check the effect.  

Rendering animation takes considerable time, so I will show you a pre-rendered video instead.  

The video does not yet support background transparency.  

Below is the saved file location.  
You can choose the video and save folder.  
This depends on where you want to save on your computer.  

All settings are done.  
Now, stop rendering.  

Watch the pre-rendered animation.  
You can see the fabric flow making the movement more realistic.  

Switch back to image view.  
Here you can see all picture/video properties.  
Click “Save.”  

If you have a unified rendering specification, save it as a .vmp file,  
so next time you open it, you can render in the same format.  

After saving, let’s make simple adjustments to properties,  
such as changing the background to red.  
Refresh.  

Open the saved file; all properties revert to previous settings.  

Next, light properties.  
Open light properties, and you can see the renderer has randomly enabled top lights.  

Next, environment settings.  
The system has 11 HDR files loaded randomly into the environment.  
Environment lighting is treated as an image format.  

Environment settings provide different lighting effects, creating various atmospheres.  

Let’s switch environments to see the effect.  

Now using a low-contrast image, lighting is even and soft.  

Switch to a high-contrast image; lighting on the model is dimmer with clear separation,  
making the image more three-dimensional.  

Next, observe how the renderer affects different environments.  
Here is a normal 3D quick snapshot.  
After enabling the renderer, lighting changes according to environment, showing different contrast effects.  
Choose an environment you prefer.  

Next, light intensity.  
Light intensity can be adjusted—the larger the value, the brighter the light.  
I’ll gradually increase intensity to maximum; the light in the window becomes very bright.  

Reduce brightness a bit.  
You can also set it to 0, which means the light is off (black).  
Normally, use the default value of 1.  

When to increase light intensity?  
For example, if clothing color is black or dark, details may be unclear.  
Increasing light intensity makes details clearer.  

You can also adjust the light angle.  
Change light angle to 45°, 90°, 180°, and observe effects separately.  

Return to default 0.  

What does the lock screen option do?  
Check lighting in the window. Front light is uniform and normal.  

Switch to back view; light is very bright.  
The lock screen option keeps lighting consistent across views,  
meaning light is linked to the camera lens.  

When enabled, light brightness stays balanced, not too bright or too dark.  
When light is off, it is hidden; when on, it shows in the 3D window.  

Hide light in the window to see effects.  

Check ground shadows.  
Refresh the window.  
Shadows appear when light is on, making the image more realistic.  

If the background is transparent, ground shadows can still be kept.  

That covers light properties.  

Next, lens properties.  

Field of view (FOV) is a photography term describing lens angle.  
Changing FOV changes lens size.  

Default FOV value is observed.  
Set FOV to 15; the object appears closer.  
Increasing FOV widens the viewing angle.  

As FOV continues to increase, the model moves away until it disappears from view.  

Reset to default FOV.  

Next, view orientation options:  
Spherical (face-to-face orientation) and Absolute (fixed orientation).  
Check differences by adjusting camera distance.  
Zoom in or out to view effects.  

Refresh image.  

Adjust horizontal angle to rotate view horizontally.  
Adjust vertical angle to rotate vertically.  
Now, the model is fully visible.  

Return to default view.  

Clipping plane controls camera near and far limits, i.e., shooting distance.  
“Near” sets the closest shooting distance.  
“Far” sets the farthest shooting distance.  

Next, actual camera settings:  
Adjust ISO, aperture, and angle of view, similar to a real camera.  

You can visit the official website’s Help Center for detailed instructions.  

Exposure controls the amount of light entering the camera and image brightness.  
Use exposure to adjust brightness effectively rather than adjusting light brightness manually.  

ISO affects image sharpness and brightness.  
You can also adjust aperture, shutter speed, focus, and focal length.  

For more details, visit the official website and search keywords.  

That concludes lens properties.  

Finally, rendering properties.  
You can open or save rendering property files here.  
Switch rendering tools as needed.  

For example, on Windows with NVIDIA graphics cards, use GPU CUDA rendering to optimize speed.  
On Mac with AMD or Intel graphics, GPU CUDA is recommended as well.  

I use an NVIDIA GPU, so I choose GPU CUDA rendering.  

Lowering GPU rendering priority means prioritizing other functions while rendering.  

You can set the maximum rendering time for a single image; default is 20 minutes.  
Rendering complex models or larger size/quality images increases rendering time.  

Set maximum rendering time accordingly.  

Next, light source and properties.  
Set language.  

We are going to use this.  
If connection is lost, we can continue.  

The quality of light source can be set to low, medium, high, or very high.  

When rendering white hair, use high or very high light source quality.  
Rendering time increases accordingly.  

This concludes the rendering introduction.  

The last feature is rendering through Close-Set.  
Click it; a dialog asks if you want to render on Close-Set.  
Click “Run.”  

A progress circle appears top right.  
After rendering, a dialog confirms success.  
Click “Confirm.”  

You will see a page to enter your ID and password.  
Select the folder location to save files.  
Click “Confirm.”  

Images are rendered and uploaded to Close-Set.  
You can click on 3D file to interact.  

Now, scroll down.  

The second row toolbar shows new 5.2 features.  
Click light source; it auto-opens the light source.  
Click again to show a dialog stating the light is already in the environment.  
Only one large environment light can be added.  

Next, add a main light.  
After clicking, the main light board appears on the 3D window floor.  
Rotate and move it using the locator.  

Adjust the light board’s position and angle.  
The line below adjusts the light angle.  

Change the light board position to better see effects.  
Turn off the light board and refresh the screen.  

The red line shows the refresh.  
Now you see the main light board effect.  

It acts like a light box in a camera.  
Adjust brightness and direction.  
Adjust width and height; increasing them increases the light area.  

Right-click to open the menu to delete, hide, or reactivate the light board.  

Deleting hides it from the 3D window.  

Next, add a ball-shaped light.  
It emits light evenly from the center with no directional bias.  

Increase intensity; higher intensity means brighter light.  
Adjust radius; larger radius means brighter light.  

Add light-sensitive pink color.  
Adjust brightness for a brighter color.  

Turn lights on/off and toggle spotlight.  
Adjust spotlight position, intensity, and angle.  

The 3D window has no floor, so lighting area is not visible.  
Add a rectangular plate in the 2D window as the floor.  
No simulation needed; it’s a simple rectangle.  

Increase particle diameter to max to reduce computer load.  
Place 3D window in the lower right of the model.  
Adjust to top view.  

Replace ground with this plate.  
Open and refresh renderer.  
Select all lights and adjust.  

After adjusting, see the spotlight area on the ground.  
Increase brightness.  
Adjust width of the illuminated area; larger width = wider light spread.  

Adjust softness of the light edge; larger value softens edges.  

Next, shadow sharpness.  
Higher value means softer shadows; lower means sharper edges.  

Turn off activation and display for now.  

Next, square light (direct light).  
It emits parallel light, like outdoor light, with no specific source.  
Adjust intensity.  

I choose light gray to brighten the light.  

Delete square light.  

Fifth light type: R1S light.  
R1S files store real brightness and shape data of actual lights.  
System has some R1S files; nine available.  

Adjust position and angle in 3D window.  
Adjust IES light intensity and color.  
Try different effects if interested.  

Finally, skylight.  
It was off before; now turned on.  
It provides large environment lighting.  

This concludes the rendering window introduction.  

At bottom right, you can choose preview window size, display at 100% or other scales.  
You can change the 2D or rendering window here.  

Back to main menu, rendering functions through color set are shown.  
High-quality 3D rendering window is the first icon in the 3D window display menu.  

That’s all for today’s live broadcast.  
Thank you for watching.  
If you have questions, please leave comments.  

I trust you will find this useful.  
See you next time.  
Thank you.  
Good evening.  
Thank you.  
You are very warm.  
Thank you for coming.  
Goodbye.  

You can watch the video on our official Bilibili account.  
It will be released in about 7 days.  

What is the difference between a rectangular lamp and a rectangular lamp?  
A rectangular lamp only shines in a certain area near the lamp board.  
A rectangular lamp is a parallel lamp visible throughout the environment.  
Unless you increase its intensity very high, it only shines in that area.  

You can download the video editor from the main menu by clicking “Video.”  
If you don’t have a video editor installed, a dialog will pop up.  
Click the link at the top to jump to the video editor download page.  

Regarding hair dye settings,  
we will have a dedicated live stream on hair dyeing and other materials on July 3.  
Follow our official WeChat account to receive updates.  

If you use custom models in OBJ or FBX format,  
you can download and use them directly in the cloud.  

As the software updates, the number of new fabrics increases.  
Initially, there were about 40 types.  
Now, version 5.2 has over 70 fabric types.  
More will come in the future.  

Thank you very much.  

If the fabric quality is too thin, it’s not recommended to measure fabric quality.  

Next Friday is the Dragon Boat Festival holiday, so no live broadcast then.  

If you don’t support GPU simulation, check if your computer needs GPU drivers.  

Today’s guest is Molly, very familiar with GPU simulation.  
Fans of GPU simulation will know Molly’s sweet voice here.  

For GPU simulation, you need to buy the GPU Simulator,  
which records stretch, curve, and other real material values.  
The system calculates electronic materials automatically,  
applying them to 3D clothing.  

For more about GPU simulation, leave a message.  
To purchase the GPU Simulator, contact us on the official website: www.clo3d.com.  

You can also reach us on Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp.  
Follow us on Instagram and Twitter.  

Do you want an official WeChat group?  
Currently, we only have groups for enterprise users.  
You can follow our official account first.  

Can oily skin buy it?  
Are you joking? Dry skin can also buy it.  

Please continue to follow our regular live streams.  
We will share tips and detailed usage instructions.  

If you haven’t subscribed to our Bilibili live account, please do so now.  
You can also follow us on Weibo and Facebook on the right side of the screen.  

If you want to learn more about the live stream, click the link on the right.  

Our live stream will end in 5 minutes.  
If you have questions, feel free to ask.  

Sorry, the live stream will end in 2 minutes at 9 o’clock.  
Thank you.  

As long as you enjoy watching, we will be happy to do more live streams with different topics.  

Due to time limits, I thought we had 5 minutes; now only 1 minute remains.  

Thank you all for watching tonight’s 8 o’clock live stream.  
Please follow our Bilibili live account.  
Subscribe if you haven’t yet.  

The live stream will end in 5 minutes.  
Looking forward to seeing you next time.  
See you next time.  
See you next time.  
Good night.  
Good night.  
Good night.  
Good night.

chunks.content: # Master Express Lesson 1: Rendering Introduction and Workflow This document covers detailed rendering functions, tools, and settings in CLO version 5.2, including the 3D window rendering engine, rendering window operations, animation and image rendering, lighting and lens properties, and advanced rendering options such as Close-Set rendering and GPU acceleration. --- ## Rendering Engine and 3D Window Rendering Modes This section explains the updated rendering engine in CLO 5.2, the differences between standard 3D window rendering, high-quality 3D rendering, and final rendering images, and how to record rotating videos with enhanced rendering. - The 3D window now includes a high-quality rendering engine introduced in version 5.2. - Access the rendering engine via the 3D window context menu; the first icon toggles high-quality rendering. - Comparison between: - Ordinary 3D window snapshot (basic rendering) - High-quality rendered 3D window snapshot - Final rendered image (highest quality) - Users can choose rendering quality based on their needs. - Rotating video recording is available under the main menu "File." - Enable high-quality rendering for better video effects. - Adjust rotation direction and duration (rotation speed inversely proportional to duration). - Recorded videos are saved in AVI format. - Thanks to 3D window optimization, rotating videos render quickly with good quality. --- ## Rendering Window Overview and Toolbar Functions This section details the rendering window interface, describing each toolbar icon’s purpose and how to use them for synchronous rendering, final rendering, image copying, and saving. - Rendering toolbar has key icons: 1. **Synchronous Rendering**: Real-time preview of rendering in the preview window. 2. **Final Rendering**: Starts final high-quality rendering after stopping synchronous rendering. - Must stop synchronous rendering before final rendering. 3. **Stop Rendering**: Interrupts ongoing rendering processes. 4. **Copy Current Image**: Copies the preview image to clipboard for pasting into other applications like Excel. 5. **Save Current Image**: Saves the preview image (not final render quality) directly from the preview window. 6. **Open Saved Folder**: Quickly access saved output files. 7. **Image/Video Properties**: Open or save rendering parameter files; adjust rendering settings for images or animations. - Final rendering produces the highest quality images saved to disk. - Stopping rendering allows users to adjust settings such as clothing color or details before completing final rendering. --- ## Image and Animation Rendering Settings This section explains how to configure views, image sizes, background options, file formats, rotation images, and animation rendering parameters. - **User-Defined Views**: - Load or save multiple camera views. - Record views by clicking the camera icon in the rendering window. - Render multiple images from saved views simultaneously. - **Image Size and Orientation**: - Supports custom sizes; example: 1920x1080 resolution. - Orientation options: vertical or horizontal. - **Background Options**: - Solid colors with or without transparency. - Use textures as backgrounds (14 texture options available). - **File Naming and Formats**: - Common formats: PNG, JPG, and an HTML file for web embedding. - **Rotation Images and Video**: - Choose number of images for rotation (e.g., 12 for full 360°).

chunks.content: - Render multiple images from saved views simultaneously. - **Image Size and Orientation**: - Supports custom sizes; example: 1920x1080 resolution. - Orientation options: vertical or horizontal. - **Background Options**: - Solid colors with or without transparency. - Use textures as backgrounds (14 texture options available). - **File Naming and Formats**: - Common formats: PNG, JPG, and an HTML file for web embedding. - **Rotation Images and Video**: - Choose number of images for rotation (e.g., 12 for full 360°). - Select rotation direction: clockwise or counterclockwise. - Optionally generate a rotation video along with images. - Adjust total rotation duration and single image frame duration. - **Animation Rendering**: - Render animations completed in animation mode. - Choose rendering area: full or play area. - Set frames per second (default 30 FPS). - Enable “Save Video” to export video files. - Note: Animation rendering takes significant time. - Background transparency is not supported in animation videos yet. --- ## Saving and Loading Rendering Properties This section covers how to save and reuse rendering settings to ensure consistency across projects. - Save rendering parameters as `.vmp` files for reuse. - Loading saved property files restores all rendering settings. - Modify properties (e.g., background color) and refresh rendering. - Opening saved files reverts to previously saved settings. - Allows standardized rendering workflows. --- ## Lighting Properties and Environment Settings This section explains lighting controls including light types, environment HDRs, intensity, angle, and shadow effects to create realistic rendering scenes. - Renderer randomly selects from 11 HDR environment images providing diverse lighting atmospheres. - Switching environments changes light contrast and model illumination. - Light intensity scale: - Default is 1. - Increase intensity for dark clothing to reveal details. - Intensity 0 turns light off. - Light angle adjustments: tested at 45°, 90°, 180°. - Lock Screen option: - Links light to camera lens for consistent brightness across views. - Ground shadows: - Appear with light enabled. - Work even with transparent backgrounds. - Multiple light types available: - **Main light board**: acts like a camera light box with adjustable position, angle, brightness, width, and height. - **Ball-shaped light**: emits omnidirectional light evenly. - **Spotlight**: directional with adjustable position, intensity, angle, and edge softness. - **Square light (direct light)**: parallel light similar to outdoor sunlight. - **R1S lights**: use real brightness and shape data for realistic lighting (nine R1S files available). - **Skylight**: provides broad environment illumination. - Light controls include toggling on/off, deleting, hiding, and reactivating lights. - Adjust shadow sharpness and softness for desired realism. --- ## Lens Properties and Camera Settings This section covers camera lens controls including field of view (FOV), orientation modes, clipping planes, and photographic settings to fine-tune render perspectives. - **Field of View (FOV)**: - Controls viewing angle. - Lower FOV (e.g., 15) zooms in making the object appear closer. - Higher FOV widens the angle, objects appear farther. - **View Orientation**: - Spherical mode: face-to-face orientation. - Absolute mode: fixed orientation regardless of camera movement.

chunks.content: --- ## Lens Properties and Camera Settings This section covers camera lens controls including field of view (FOV), orientation modes, clipping planes, and photographic settings to fine-tune render perspectives. - **Field of View (FOV)**: - Controls viewing angle. - Lower FOV (e.g., 15) zooms in making the object appear closer. - Higher FOV widens the angle, objects appear farther. - **View Orientation**: - Spherical mode: face-to-face orientation. - Absolute mode: fixed orientation regardless of camera movement. - **Camera Controls**: - Horizontal and vertical angle adjustments to rotate view. - Clipping planes control near and far limits of camera shooting distance. - **Camera Parameters**: - ISO: affects image brightness and sharpness. - Aperture, shutter speed, focus, and focal length simulate real camera settings. - Exposure adjusts overall image brightness more effectively than light brightness alone. - Detailed camera setting instructions available on the official CLO Help Center. --- ## Rendering Properties and GPU Acceleration This section explains rendering engine options, GPU support, rendering time limits, and light source quality settings to optimize rendering performance. - Save and load rendering property files. - Switch rendering engines: - Windows with NVIDIA GPUs: use GPU CUDA rendering for speed optimization. - Mac with AMD or Intel GPUs: GPU CUDA rendering recommended. - GPU rendering priority can be lowered to prioritize other system functions. - Maximum rendering time per image is configurable (default 20 minutes). - Complex models or higher resolution/quality increase rendering time. - Light source quality settings: - Low, medium, high, very high. - Rendering white hair requires high or very high quality, increasing rendering time. - Rendering can resume automatically if connection is lost. --- ## Close-Set Rendering and Cloud Upload This section outlines the Close-Set rendering feature for cloud-based rendering and file upload. - Click “Close-Set” to start cloud rendering. - Progress indicator shown in top-right corner. - Upon completion, confirmation dialog appears. - User logs in with ID and password. - Select folder location to save files. - Rendered images are uploaded to Close-Set. - Users can interact with 3D files online. --- ## Additional Features in Version 5.2 This section highlights new rendering features introduced in CLO 5.2 related to lighting tools and user interface enhancements. - Second toolbar row introduces new version 5.2 lighting features. - Only one large environment light can be added at a time. - Main light board: - Added on 3D window floor. - Movable and rotatable with locator. - Adjust brightness, direction, width, and height to simulate a light box. - Ball-shaped light for omnidirectional illumination. - Spotlight with adjustable position, intensity, angle, and edge softness. - Ground plane can be added in the 2D window as a simple rectangle for lighting effects. - Adjust particle diameter to reduce computer load. - Shadow sharpness and softness controls. - Square light emits parallel outdoor-like light. - R1S lights provide realistic brightness and shape data. - Skylight provides broad ambient lighting. - Preview window size adjustable (100% scale or others).

markdown_content: # Master Express Lesson 1: Rendering Introduction and Workflow This document covers detailed rendering functions, tools, and settings in CLO version 5.2, including the 3D window rendering engine, rendering window operations, animation and image rendering, lighting and lens properties, and advanced rendering options such as Close-Set rendering and GPU acceleration. --- ## Rendering Engine and 3D Window Rendering Modes This section explains the updated rendering engine in CLO 5.2, the differences between standard 3D window rendering, high-quality 3D rendering, and final rendering images, and how to record rotating videos with enhanced rendering. - The 3D window now includes a high-quality rendering engine introduced in version 5.2. - Access the rendering engine via the 3D window context menu; the first icon toggles high-quality rendering. - Comparison between: - Ordinary 3D window snapshot (basic rendering) - High-quality rendered 3D window snapshot - Final rendered image (highest quality) - Users can choose rendering quality based on their needs. - Rotating video recording is available under the main menu "File." - Enable high-quality rendering for better video effects. - Adjust rotation direction and duration (rotation speed inversely proportional to duration). - Recorded videos are saved in AVI format. - Thanks to 3D window optimization, rotating videos render quickly with good quality. --- ## Rendering Window Overview and Toolbar Functions This section details the rendering window interface, describing each toolbar icon’s purpose and how to use them for synchronous rendering, final rendering, image copying, and saving. - Rendering toolbar has key icons: 1. **Synchronous Rendering**: Real-time preview of rendering in the preview window. 2. **Final Rendering**: Starts final high-quality rendering after stopping synchronous rendering. - Must stop synchronous rendering before final rendering. 3. **Stop Rendering**: Interrupts ongoing rendering processes. 4. **Copy Current Image**: Copies the preview image to clipboard for pasting into other applications like Excel. 5. **Save Current Image**: Saves the preview image (not final render quality) directly from the preview window. 6. **Open Saved Folder**: Quickly access saved output files. 7. **Image/Video Properties**: Open or save rendering parameter files; adjust rendering settings for images or animations. - Final rendering produces the highest quality images saved to disk. - Stopping rendering allows users to adjust settings such as clothing color or details before completing final rendering. --- ## Image and Animation Rendering Settings This section explains how to configure views, image sizes, background options, file formats, rotation images, and animation rendering parameters. - **User-Defined Views**: - Load or save multiple camera views. - Record views by clicking the camera icon in the rendering window. - Render multiple images from saved views simultaneously. - **Image Size and Orientation**: - Supports custom sizes; example: 1920x1080 resolution. - Orientation options: vertical or horizontal. - **Background Options**: - Solid colors with or without transparency. - Use textures as backgrounds (14 texture options available). - **File Naming and Formats**: - Common formats: PNG, JPG, and an HTML file for web embedding. - **Rotation Images and Video**: - Choose number of images for rotation (e.g., 12 for full 360°). - Select rotation direction: clockwise or counterclockwise. - Optionally generate a rotation video along with images. - Adjust total rotation duration and single image frame duration. - **Animation Rendering**: - Render animations completed in animation mode. - Choose rendering area: full or play area. - Set frames per second (default 30 FPS). - Enable “Save Video” to export video files. - Note: Animation rendering takes significant time. - Background transparency is not supported in animation videos yet. --- ## Saving and Loading Rendering Properties This section covers how to save and reuse rendering settings to ensure consistency across projects. - Save rendering parameters as `.vmp` files for reuse. - Loading saved property files restores all rendering settings. - Modify properties (e.g., background color) and refresh rendering. - Opening saved files reverts to previously saved settings. - Allows standardized rendering workflows. --- ## Lighting Properties and Environment Settings This section explains lighting controls including light types, environment HDRs, intensity, angle, and shadow effects to create realistic rendering scenes. - Renderer randomly selects from 11 HDR environment images providing diverse lighting atmospheres. - Switching environments changes light contrast and model illumination. - Light intensity scale: - Default is 1. - Increase intensity for dark clothing to reveal details. - Intensity 0 turns light off. - Light angle adjustments: tested at 45°, 90°, 180°. - Lock Screen option: - Links light to camera lens for consistent brightness across views. - Ground shadows: - Appear with light enabled. - Work even with transparent backgrounds. - Multiple light types available: - **Main light board**: acts like a camera light box with adjustable position, angle, brightness, width, and height. - **Ball-shaped light**: emits omnidirectional light evenly. - **Spotlight**: directional with adjustable position, intensity, angle, and edge softness. - **Square light (direct light)**: parallel light similar to outdoor sunlight. - **R1S lights**: use real brightness and shape data for realistic lighting (nine R1S files available). - **Skylight**: provides broad environment illumination. - Light controls include toggling on/off, deleting, hiding, and reactivating lights. - Adjust shadow sharpness and softness for desired realism. --- ## Lens Properties and Camera Settings This section covers camera lens controls including field of view (FOV), orientation modes, clipping planes, and photographic settings to fine-tune render perspectives. - **Field of View (FOV)**: - Controls viewing angle. - Lower FOV (e.g., 15) zooms in making the object appear closer. - Higher FOV widens the angle, objects appear farther. - **View Orientation**: - Spherical mode: face-to-face orientation. - Absolute mode: fixed orientation regardless of camera movement. - **Camera Controls**: - Horizontal and vertical angle adjustments to rotate view. - Clipping planes control near and far limits of camera shooting distance. - **Camera Parameters**: - ISO: affects image brightness and sharpness. - Aperture, shutter speed, focus, and focal length simulate real camera settings. - Exposure adjusts overall image brightness more effectively than light brightness alone. - Detailed camera setting instructions available on the official CLO Help Center. --- ## Rendering Properties and GPU Acceleration This section explains rendering engine options, GPU support, rendering time limits, and light source quality settings to optimize rendering performance. - Save and load rendering property files. - Switch rendering engines: - Windows with NVIDIA GPUs: use GPU CUDA rendering for speed optimization. - Mac with AMD or Intel GPUs: GPU CUDA rendering recommended. - GPU rendering priority can be lowered to prioritize other system functions. - Maximum rendering time per image is configurable (default 20 minutes). - Complex models or higher resolution/quality increase rendering time. - Light source quality settings: - Low, medium, high, very high. - Rendering white hair requires high or very high quality, increasing rendering time. - Rendering can resume automatically if connection is lost. --- ## Close-Set Rendering and Cloud Upload This section outlines the Close-Set rendering feature for cloud-based rendering and file upload. - Click “Close-Set” to start cloud rendering. - Progress indicator shown in top-right corner. - Upon completion, confirmation dialog appears. - User logs in with ID and password. - Select folder location to save files. - Rendered images are uploaded to Close-Set. - Users can interact with 3D files online. --- ## Additional Features in Version 5.2 This section highlights new rendering features introduced in CLO 5.2 related to lighting tools and user interface enhancements. - Second toolbar row introduces new version 5.2 lighting features. - Only one large environment light can be added at a time. - Main light board: - Added on 3D window floor. - Movable and rotatable with locator. - Adjust brightness, direction, width, and height to simulate a light box. - Ball-shaped light for omnidirectional illumination. - Spotlight with adjustable position, intensity, angle, and edge softness. - Ground plane can be added in the 2D window as a simple rectangle for lighting effects. - Adjust particle diameter to reduce computer load. - Shadow sharpness and softness controls. - Square light emits parallel outdoor-like light. - R1S lights provide realistic brightness and shape data. - Skylight provides broad ambient lighting. - Preview window size adjustable (100% scale or others). - Toggle display between 2D and rendering windows. --- ## Fabric and GPU Simulation Notes This section provides insights into fabric types, GPU simulation requirements, and upcoming content. - Version 5.2 includes over 70 fabric types, up from about 40 initially. - Thin fabrics are not recommended for fabric quality measurement. - GPU simulation requires purchasing the GPU Simulator module. - Records stretch, curve, and real material properties. - Automatically applies electronic materials to 3D clothing. - GPU Simulator available for purchase at www.clo3d.com. - GPU simulation support requires updated GPU drivers. - Dedicated live stream on hair dyeing and materials scheduled
